title: To God we return
hook: Muslims say "to God we belong and to God we return" on hearing of a loss

segments.voice: Yesterday: the woman at the grave, and patience at the first stroke. Your line was sabr. Did you find one breath before the first reply? Today, the words the Quran puts in the mouths of the steadfast. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

The phone lights up with a message from a Muslim friend: her grandmother has died. Under it, the replies start arriving, one after another, and they begin with the same Arabic phrase, or its initials. The phrase is inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Different people, different spellings, the same sentence. Muslims say it on hearing of a death, and of other losses too. It isn't a condolence card. It's a verse. Today, where the line comes from: yesterday's passage.
screen: `A MESSAGE: HER GRANDMOTHER HAS DIED.` → `THE SAME SENTENCE, OVER AND OVER.` → `NOT A CARD. A VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes from. Yesterday's verses said people will be tried with fear and loss, and gave good news to the steadfast. The next verse describes them: they are those "Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That's Pickthall's English. The patient are known by what they say. Second, two halves. We are God's: in this reading, whatever was lost was never simply owned. Not the money, not the health, not even the people we love. And unto Him we are returning: the one who has died has gone back where everyone is going. The sentence holds the loss and the hope in a single breath. Third, a widow's story. In the hadith collection of Muslim, Umm Salama tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that someone struck by a loss should say this verse, and ask God for reward in the affliction and something better in its place. When her husband Abu Salama died, she said it, and wondered who could be better than him. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. She said it before she could imagine any answer. Fourth, looking back. This is the end of a week on suffering. Two grieving sisters with the same sentence, and Jesus weeping with them. A wish, said plainly in a garden. The cross, read as company. A thorn that stayed. Ease, promised twice. Patience at the first stroke. And now a sentence for the moment the news arrives. Again and again this week, the texts give people words to say in the worst moment, and leave the why unanswered.
screen: `THE STEADFAST ARE KNOWN BY WHAT THEY SAY.` · `WE ARE GOD'S. WE ARE RETURNING.` · `UMM SALAMA SAID IT.` · `A WEEK OF WORDS FOR SUFFERING.` · then, large: `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, hands in your lap. Think of something you once called yours and no longer have: a person, a home, a job, the body you had at twenty. Name it silently, by its plain name. Now try the verse's shape in your own words, if it fits for you: first, where it came from, then, where it has gone. Or simply: it was given; it is gone; it mattered. If you're Muslim, or if you wish, you can say the verse itself over it. Then let the words go quiet, and let the loss stay a while in the silence after them. The bell holds the time.
To God we return: from the Quran, said by Muslims on hearing of a loss. We are God's, and to Him we are returning. Today's word.
Your line: to god we return. Today, honor one loss in words: write it, say it to someone, or speak it quietly to yourself. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

The hook's Muslim friend and group chat are the script's own scene. Hook describes one scene, not a statistic.

Umm Salama's hadith (Sahih Muslim 918) paraphrased: the Prophet taught that one afflicted should say the verse and 'O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in exchange'; she said it at Abu Salama's death, wondered who could be better, and the Prophet later proposed. The supplication is described, not quoted or newly written. Confirm numbering and details.
